q: CH≡C–CH2–CH2–CH=CH2, IUPAC name of the compound is
question: CH≡C–CH2–CH2–CH=CH2, IUPAC name of the compound is
solution:
Compound: $CH \equiv C - CH_2 - CH_2 - CH = CH_2$

The longest continuous carbon chain containing both multiple bonds has 6 carbon atoms. Therefore, the root word is hex.

According to IUPAC rules, the principal chain must be numbered to give the lowest possible set of locants to the multiple bonds.

  • Numbering from left to right gives the locants 1 and 5.

  • Numbering from right to left also gives the locants 1 and 5.

When the set of locants is identical from both directions, the double bond is given preference over the triple bond and receives the lower number. Thus, the correct numbering is from right to left:

$C^6H \equiv C^5 - C^4H_2 - C^3H_2 - C^2H = C^1H_2$

  • The double bond is at position 1: -1-en (the terminal 'e' of 'ene' is dropped because the next suffix begins with the letter 'y').

  • The triple bond is at position 5: -5-yne.

Combining these parts, the correct IUPAC name is Hex-1-en-5-yne.

This corresponds to Option D.

question: 3-methyl penta-1,3-diene is
solution:
1. The root word penta tells us that the longest continuous carbon chain contains $5$ carbon atoms.

  2. The suffix -1,3-diene means there are two double bonds: one starting at carbon-1 ($C_1$) and the other starting at carbon-3 ($C_3$).

  3. The prefix 3-methyl shows that a methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$) is attached to carbon-3.

Let us write the carbon chain and number it from right to left or left to right such that the double bonds get the lowest locants:

\overset{5}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3 - \overset{4}{\text{C}}\text{H} = \overset{3}{\text{C}}(\text{CH}_3) - \overset{2}{\text{C}}\text{H} = \overset{1}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2

Numbering from the right gives:

  • Double bonds at $C_1$ and $C_3$.

  • A methyl branch at $C_3$.

Writing this in condensed form gives:

\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2

Looking at the given options:

  • Option A: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3$ has only one double bond (hex-1-ene).

  • Option B: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ has only one double bond (3-methylpent-1-ene).

  • Option C: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ matches our derived structure.

  • Option D: $\text{CH}_3=\text{CH}=\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ has incorrect carbon valencies.

Therefore, the correct choice is Option C.

question: The correct IUPAC name for the compound is :
solution:
1. Selection of the Principal Carbon Chain:

  • The principal chain must contain the maximum number of principal functional groups, which in this case is the carbon-carbon double bond ($\mathrm{C=C}$).

  • This means the compound must be named as an alkene, ruling out naming it as an alkane (heptane).

  • Starting from the double bond, the chain contains carbons $\text{C}_1$ and $\text{C}_2$. At carbon-3 ($\text{C}_3$), the chain branches.

  • If we trace the chain toward the left, we get a 6-carbon chain with only one substituent at $\text{C}_3$, which is a $(1\text{-ethylpropyl})$ group.

  • If we trace the chain toward the right, we also get a 6-carbon chain ($\text{hex-1-ene}$), but it gives two simpler substituents: a propyl group at $\text{C}_3$ and an ethyl group at $\text{C}_4$.

  • According to IUPAC rules, when two chains have the same length and contain the double bond, the one with the greater number of substituents is selected as the parent chain. Therefore, the 6-carbon chain with two substituents is the correct parent chain.

  1. Numbering the Chain:

  • Numbering begins from the end that gives the lowest locant to the double bond:

    \text{C}_1=\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3-\text{C}_4-\text{C}_5-\text{C}_6

  • The double bond is at position $1$ ($\text{hex-1-ene}$).

  1. Identifying and Numbering the Substituents:

  • An ethyl group ($-\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$) is attached at carbon-4.

  • A propyl group ($-\mathrm{CH_2CH_2CH_3}$) is attached at carbon-3.

  1. Alphabetical Arrangement:

  • Arranging the substituents alphabetically ("ethyl" before "propyl") gives:

    \text{4-ethyl-3-propylhex-1-ene}

Therefore, the correct choice is Option A.

1+6=\boxed{7}.

question:
If the given IUPAC name of following compounds.

$\operatorname{are}(A) \rightarrow x$-hexen-y-yne

(B) →P-hexen-Q-yne

The value of $x+y+P-Q$ will be ……
solution:
To find the values of $x$, $y$, $P$, and $Q$, we apply the IUPAC nomenclature rules for naming hydrocarbons containing both double and triple bonds.

For Compound (A):

\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3

The principal carbon chain contains $6$ carbon atoms (hex).

We determine the numbering of the chain:

  • Numbering from left to right gives locant $2$ to the double bond and locant $4$ to the triple bond: $(2, 4)$.

  • Numbering from right to left gives locant $2$ to the triple bond and locant $4$ to the double bond: $(2, 4)$.

Since both directions yield the same set of locants, preference is given to the double bond to have the lower locant.

Therefore, numbering proceeds from left to right:

\overset{1}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3-\overset{2}{\text{C}}\text{H}=\overset{3}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\overset{4}{\text{C}}\equiv\overset{5}{\text{C}}-\overset{6}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3

The IUPAC name is 2-hexen-4-yne (or hex-2-en-4-yne).

  • $x = 2$

  • $y = 4$

For Compound (B):

\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2

This chain also contains $6$ carbon atoms.

  • Numbering from left to right gives locants $(1, 5)$, with the triple bond at position $1$.

  • Numbering from right to left gives locants $(1, 5)$, with the double bond at position $1$.

Again, the set of locants is identical from both ends. When a double bond and a triple bond compete for the same position numbers, the double bond gets the lower locant.

Thus, the chain is numbered from right to left:

\overset{6}{\text{C}}\text{H}\equiv\overset{5}{\text{C}}-\overset{4}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\overset{3}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\overset{2}{\text{C}}\text{H}=\overset{1}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2

The IUPAC name is 1-hexen-5-yne (or hex-1-en-5-yne).

  • $P = 1$

  • $Q = 5$

Now, substituting these values into the required expression:

x + y + P - Q = 2 + 4 + 1 - 5 = 2

q:
The number of IUPAC names possible with molecular

formula $C_6H_{10}$ among following names is ……

I. 2-hexyne

II. 3-hexyne

III. 4-methyl-2-hexyne

IV. 3-cyclopropylpropyne
question:
The number of IUPAC names possible with molecular

formula $C_6H_{10}$ among following names is ……

I. 2-hexyne

II. 3-hexyne

III. 4-methyl-2-hexyne

IV. 3-cyclopropylpropyne
solution:
For the molecular formula $C_6H_{10}$, the degree of unsaturation is:

\text{Degree of unsaturation}=\frac{2C+2-H}{2}

=\frac{2(6)+2-10}{2} =\frac{4}{2}=2

So $C_6H_{10}$ can represent an alkyne with one triple bond, because one triple bond gives two degrees of unsaturation.

Now check each name.

I. $2$-hexyne has $6$ carbon atoms and one triple bond.

For an open-chain alkyne,

C_nH_{2n-2}

For $n=6$,

C_6H_{10}

So I is possible.

II. $3$-hexyne also has $6$ carbon atoms and one triple bond.

Its formula is also:

C_6H_{10}

So II is possible.

III. $4$-methyl-$2$-hexyne has $6+1=7$ carbon atoms.

So its formula will not be $C_6H_{10}$. It will be $C_7H_{12}$.

So III is not possible.

IV. $3$-cyclopropylpropyne has a triple bond and also a ring.

Triple bond gives $2$ degrees of unsaturation, and the ring gives $1$ more. Total degree of unsaturation becomes $3$.

For $6$ carbons and degree of unsaturation $3$:

H = 2(6)+2-2(3)=14-6=8

So its formula is:

C_6H_8

So IV is not possible.

Hence, only I and II have molecular formula $C_6H_{10}$.

\boxed{2}
explanation:
For the molecular formula $C_6H_{10}$, the degree of unsaturation is:

\text{Degree of unsaturation}=\frac{2C+2-H}{2}

=\frac{2(6)+2-10}{2} =\frac{4}{2}=2

So $C_6H_{10}$ can represent an alkyne with one triple bond, because one triple bond gives two degrees of unsaturation.

Now check each name.

I. $2$-hexyne has $6$ carbon atoms and one triple bond.

For an open-chain alkyne,

C_nH_{2n-2}

For $n=6$,

C_6H_{10}

So I is possible.

II. $3$-hexyne also has $6$ carbon atoms and one triple bond.

Its formula is also:

C_6H_{10}

So II is possible.

III. $4$-methyl-$2$-hexyne has $6+1=7$ carbon atoms.

So its formula will not be $C_6H_{10}$. It will be $C_7H_{12}$.

So III is not possible.

IV. $3$-cyclopropylpropyne has a triple bond and also a ring.

Triple bond gives $2$ degrees of unsaturation, and the ring gives $1$ more. Total degree of unsaturation becomes $3$.

For $6$ carbons and degree of unsaturation $3$:

H = 2(6)+2-2(3)=14-6=8

So its formula is:

C_6H_8

So IV is not possible.

Hence, only I and II have molecular formula $C_6H_{10}$.

\boxed{2}

question: How many $s p$-hybridized C atoms are in the given molecule?
solution:
Each carbon atom in a carbon–carbon triple bond is $sp$-hybridized because it has two regions of electron density.

The molecule has one $\mathrm{C\equiv C}$ bond at the left end, giving two $sp$-hybridized carbon atoms. The carbons in the double bond at the right end are $sp^2$-hybridized.
